sources.title: Book request #184: 'Nix from First Principles' syllabus and editorial principles
Dolstra, The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model (2006)
Software Sustainability Institute: Reproducible Environments With Nix

structure.rationale: The order follows the requester's syllabus and its central question — how a description becomes a package, a dev environment, or a system. It goes: motivation and map, the store, the language, derivations and the build lifecycle, packaging and customization, dev environments and flakes, real applications and CI, then modules, Home Manager and NixOS (kept optional until late), and finally debugging, a capstone and contributing. Each chapter keeps the requester's seven-beat rhythm. Note: web fetches (nix.dev, Nix manual) were refused by the proxy during scaffolding, so no external sources were consulted yet; each concept page must fetch and record its sources before writing.
structure.audience: Developers comfortable with a terminal, git, one programming language and basic build/dependency workflows; no prior Nix or NixOS knowledge.

claims.text: Conventional package managers install into shared global locations (e.g. /usr/lib), so two programs needing different versions of one library compete for the same path; this is the 'dependency hell' Nix was designed to avoid.
Nix stores each package under a path containing a hash of all its inputs, so versions coexist side by side and upgrades/rollbacks are atomic.

Builds and install scripts often depend on undeclared things on the host (tools on PATH, system libraries, env vars, locale, OS version); these hidden assumptions are the usual cause of 'works on my machine'.

Recording what is installed (a snapshot such as pip freeze or a package list) lists results, not the inputs and steps that produced them, and usually omits the OS-level tools and libraries; a description states what should be present and how it is made.
Language lock files (mix.lock, Cargo.lock) pin language libraries but not the compiler, OS libraries or tools outside the language's package manager.
Nix builds run in a sandbox (default on Linux, not default on macOS) so undeclared dependencies fail loudly instead of silently working.

pitfalls: Do not claim Nix makes everything perfectly reproducible; later chapters cover where it breaks down.
